A Samnite settlement occupying a strategic location in the valley of the Sangro river.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 G4 Amalfitana Civitas
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 E3 Ad Flexum
Ad Medias was a mutatio on the ancient Via Appia. It was located at the halfway point of the so-called Decennovium.
Ad Turres Albas lay on the Via Severiana, midway between Circeii and Astura.
An ancient settlement (modern Isernia in Italy)

The toponym Amplero refers to an archaeological area located to the northeast of Collelongo (L'Aquila) in Italy. The Institute of Archaeology at the University of Pisa conducted fieldwork at the site in 1969-1971.

A Hernican hill town that formed part of a sixth-century B.C. defensive league against Volscian and Samnite aggression and allied itself to Tarquinius Superbus. Rome eventually took Aletrium in 306 B.C.; by the first century B.C., the site was a Roman municipium.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 F4 Ad Quartum
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 F4 Aequana

A Roman villa at Anguillara Sabazia that may have been built in order to take advantage of mineral springs. The villa dates to the Late Republican period but has only been partially excavated. A large hemicycle with ambulatio is extant; this feature may have been coordinated with the villa's garden.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 F2 Ad Rotas/Rotae
An ancient town of either Oscan or Samnite origin situated in the Volturno river valley.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 F4 Afragola
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 E1 Agellum
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 D3 Ad Turres
A town of the Marsi in the valley of the Liris river.
Abellinum was a settlement of the Hirpini in Campania.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 F2 Duronia
A villa of the emperor Domitian located in the area of Circeii.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 E1 *Lavernae
A Latin colony founded ca. 312 B.C. along the Via Latina. The site was sacked by Samnites (ca. 294 B.C.) and subsequently by Hannibal (212 B.C.). It received Roman municipal status in 90 B.C.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 E2 Fregellanum
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 F2 Frosolone
Fabrateria Vetus was a Volscian settlement that surrendered to Rome in 424 B.C.
Hamae is an ancient site of Campania located between Capua and Cumae, although its precise location is difficult to fix. The people of Capua gathered there for a solemn religious festival.
At Grottacce are the remains of a Roman seaside villa or villa maritima.
A Hernican town along the Via Latina that the Romans captured in 364 B.C. Later in the Republican period (after 195 B.C.) the city received Roman municipal status.
A fortified ancient hilltop, Ferrazzano is usually identified as a Samnite site.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 E1 Giurlanda
Fagifulae was a center of the Pentrian Samnites.

An Imperial villa excavated by A. Maiuri in the 1930s, Damecuta was connected to the Iulio-Claudian emperors. The construction of later Medieval and Bourbon fortifications on the site significantly damaged the ancient remains. The Medieval Damecuta tower stands atop part of the Roman villa.

Fregellae was a city of Latium Adjectum that became a Roman colony in 328 B.C., but was subsequently captured by the Samnites; a Roman presence was re-established in 313 B.C. Loyal to Rome during the Second Punic War, Fregellae revolted in 125 B.C. and the site was razed.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 F4 ‘Invinias’
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 E2 La Giostra
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 G4 Fratte
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 F1 ‘Iovis Lareni’
Kupelternum/Cubulteria was an ancient Samnite settlement.
An ancient settlement of Campania, Cumae was the first Greek colony established on the Italian mainland in the eighth century BC.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 E2 Gioia dei Marsi
An ancient Roman town of Campania destroyed by the eruption of Mt. Vesuvius in A.D. 79. Named as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

Fabrateria Nova received a Roman colony in 124 B.C. that was dispatched by Caius Gracchus. The relationship between Fabrateria Nova and the earlier Volscian site of Fabrateria Vetus remains unclear. The favored location for Fabrateria Nova is at S. Giovanni Incarico, where the Liri and Sacco rivers intersect.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 E3 Faustianum?
A Roman municipium founded in 87 BC after the Social War, Iuvanum sits on the site of a pre-existing Samnite settlement that occupies an upland plateau.
The Fanum Dianae Tifatinae located on the slopes of Mt. Tifata in Campania.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 44 C1 Cretone
Frusino (modern Frosinone) was a town in Latium along the Via Latina that was originally a Volscian settlement.
The site of a villa associated with Lucius Vitruvius Mamurra.

A large fanum sacred to ‘Herculis Rani’? at Campochiaro, the name of which is then preserved in the station mentioned on the Peutinger Table. Scholars like A. La Regina support linking this fanum to a place mentioned by Livy, although see discussion by Oakley.
Fundi achieved civitas sine suffragio after the Latin War in 338 B.C.
An important town of the Ager Falernus, not to be confused with Forum Popili, the modern Polla.
A pre-Roman and Roman settlement of Samnium.
An ancient settlement of likely Greek origin along the Via Appia. Cicero was assassinated near Formiae (now Formia) in 43 B.C.
A maritime city of Campania situated on the Phlegrean Peninsula. The settlement started as a Greek colony and became a Roman colony under the name Puteoli in 194 B.C.

The Lucus Furrinae or Syrian Sanctuary is a sanctuary site on the Janiculum Hill in Rome. The first known construction at the site took place during the late first century CE and it remained in use until the mid-fourth century CE.
A ruined Romano-British villa located near Hitchin, Hertfordshire, England, in the valley of the River Purwell.
The findspot for a cuneiform inscription, possibly ancient KI.KAL.
City 30 km west of Jerusalem inhabited from the Bronze Age until its destruction in 701 CE.
Neolithic site in Syria with signs of habitation dated to the 7th-6th millennia BCE.

Minoan tomb in the Mesara Plain in south-central Crete constructed during the Early Minoan I period (ca. 3100-2650 BCE) and expanded later in the Prepalatial and Protopalatial periods (through 1700 BCE).

A sanctuary of Aphrodite Ourania ("Heavenly") in Athens, on the Panathenaic Way as it entered the Athenian Agora. It consisted of an altar built around 500 BC and a temple built in the early first century AD. The Late Roman Stoa was built over the top of it in the fifth century AD.
Altar and sanctuary of Aphrodite Ourania
Settlement site between Gilat and Beer Sheva in the Negev in Israel. This site was inhabited during the Chalcolithic period.
Settlement site near the Georgian village Edisa in South Ossetia. Archaeological remains, including burials, were found in this site dating from the 11th-12th centuries CE.
Remains of an extensive urban villa were discovered in 1886 during construction work at the intersection of what is now the Via Cavour and the Via dei Quattro Cantori.

Podere Marzuolo was the site of Roman pottery production from the first century B.C. until the early fourth century A.D. The site has yielded evidence for the production of terra sigillata pottery as well as evidence of blacksmithing.

Zalu Ab (also Romanized as Zālū Āb and Zālūāb) is a village in Zalu Ab Rural District, in the Central District of Ravansar County, Kermanshah Province, Iran. Several ancient objects, including a bronze bowl of a Chaldean tribal leader, are reported to have been discovered in this rural Iranian village.

Site on the Red Sea Coast in Egypt, used in the Fourth Dynasty as a port for importing turquoise and copper from Sinai. The oldest surviving papyrus from Egypt, dated during the reign of Khufu (26th century BCE), was found at the site.
An ancient fortress located in Beit Sahour, in the district of Bethlehem in Palestine.
Village in Iran inhabited since the 6th millennium BCE.

The remains of a long, early Imperial-period Roman cryptoporticus at Beneventum that was re-used in the Middle Ages. It is situated between the modern San Lorenzo district and the rural area of Cellarulo, near the Basilica of the Madonna delle Grazie in Benevento, Italy.
The modern-day site of a Roman-British settlement dates from the second to fourth centuries AD.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 no. 43 (villas on Via Castrimeniense)
The so-called Tomb of Clodius along the Via Appia near Castel Gandolfo.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 E2 no. 62 (temple NW Anagnia)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 no. 26 (villa at Giardinetti)
Roman Villa at Lago di Nemi
A Roman Villa on the shores of Lago di Nemi.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 no. 33 (forts near Aefula)

Since antiquity, the 6,000-ha estate at Castelporziano has been an elite seaside compound. Where a modern pleasure villa for the Italian president now sits are remains of Roman villas on the Laurentine shore; these remains have been the object of continued study since 1983.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D3 no. 57 (villa near Norba)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D3 no. 56 (temple at Algidus M.)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C3 no. 52 (temple near Ardea)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 no. 31 (bridge over R. Acquoria, temple and quarries)
Road station at Foce del Fosso Grande
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C3 no. 51 (road station at Foce del Fosso Grande)
A villa rustica located near the coast, southwest of Ardea.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 no. 30 (tombs near Villa Adriana)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 E3 no. 61 (cult place near Trerus fl.)

Lugli describes the remains of a sumptuous, porticoed villa in the Doric order facing onto the Alban lake. Marzano clarifies Lugli's earlier summary of the site, which was in turn based on observations made in 1912. The remains of the villa include a 200-m long portico on two levels. About 260 m from the portico are the remains of a cistern in opus reticulatum. Chiarucci documented a structure with five barrel-vaulted rooms of unclear function. Lugli's initial report suggests that this late republican villa was eventually incorporated into the Villa of Domitian.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 no. 25 (settlement and villa at Colle dello Stinco)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 no. 41 (villa near Praeneste)

A site to the west of modern Praeneste in Italy where surface material, remains of structures, and graves were discovered in the 19th century. These finds provide evidence for a settlement possibly dating to as early as the fifth or fourth century BCE but with likely occupation throughout the subsequent Roman period.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 no. 24 (villa, NW Pantano Secco)

A Roman villa located at Vigna Spinabella and included in the Barrington Atlas. In the Barrington Atlas directory, this place is included as a "Numbered Feature" and not given a specific title. It is assigned number 44 on BAtlas map 43 C2.
The platform, including cryptoporticus, of a republican period villa originally dating to the first century B.C. with evidence for second century A.D. renovations.
Temple of Castor and Pollux, Cora
The Temple of Castor and Pollux at Cora was originally built between the fourth and the second centuries B.C. The partially extant architrave carries an inscription of the first century B.C.
A siege camp dating to the Roman siege of the fortress of Masada in A.D. 72.
The site of a Roman fort in Wales occupied during the late first and early second centuries A.D.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 no. 12 (temple at EUR)
A villa with beginnings in the early Republican period, continuing in use to the middle Imperial period.
A tuff quarry located at Castelporziano, to the east of Ostia Antica.
Unnamed villas and a tomb near Pons Mulvius
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 no. 9 (villas (2) and tomb near Pons Mulvius)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C1 no. 18 (tomb near Nomentum)
Roman villa and aqueduct at Ponte delle Sette Miglia
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 no. 22 (villa and aqueduct at Ponte delle Sette Miglia)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 A2 no. 1 (cemeteries around Caere)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 no. 23 (villa and aqueduct at Vermicino)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 no. 19 (villa near S. Sinforosa)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 no. 7 (villa N Fidenae)
A burial ground for the the Christian martyrs Gordianus, Epimachus, and Apronianus at the seventh mile of the Via Latina.
Parco delle Tombe di via Latina
A cluster of Roman Imperial tombs along the Via Latina excavated in the nineteenth century.

A farming village southeast of Amman, Jordan, inhabited from the late Neolithic Period through the sixth century BCE, and briefly inhabited again from the eleventh-thirteenth centuries; now the site of the modern town of Sahab.
A fortified Etruscan site located in the territory of Vulci.
Rowberrow Camp is the site of an Iron Age defended settlement.
Maes Knoll hill fort is an Iron Age hillfort in Somerset, England.
Hod Hill is the site of a large, rectangular Iron Age hill fort. After the Roman conquest, Romans occupied the hill-fort.

The area on the northeast side of the Piana di Himera is delimited by walls and contains four religious buildings (temples A, B, C, and D), probably dedicated to Athena. The foundations are still visible in the archaeological site of Himera.
An oppidum of the Castro Culture.
Find place for stone objects with Urartian inscriptions.
Barbury Castle is an Iron Age hill fort in Wiltshire, England.
A Medieval church on the island of Sardinia that is dated to 1133.
A necropolis of the early Dilmun culture, dating to the second millennium B.C.
Temple to Ramesses II at Abu Simbel

The larger of the two temples at Abu Simbel, dedicated to the triad of Amun, Ra-Horakhty, and Ptah, as well as the deified Ramesses II. The temple was relocated between 1964 and 1968 to prevent its submersion under Lake Nasser after the construction of the Aswan High Dam.
An Early Neolithic settlement that is now submerged beneath the waters of Lake Bracciano. Settlement activity begins ca. 5750 BCE.
Tomb of the Five Chairs, Caere
An Etruscan tomb at Caere dated ca. 625-600 B.C.
La Rustica was a Latin site located along the Via Collatina.
An archaeological site located at the midpoint of the Via Tiburtina linking Rome and Tibur.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 Tor de’ Cenci

The small hill that is known as "Il Poggio di Serrone di Bove" is located in the hinterland of ancient Norba and was the site of ancient settlement activity. Architectural remains on the site include those of a polygonal masonry sub-struction or platform as well as an ancient roadway that may be part of the road tract from Norba to Cora.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 E2 Sacro Speco

The so-called "Archi di San Lidano" are the remains of a Roman stone bridge in the Pontine plain, near the modern locality of Sezze Scalo. The bridge likely dates originally to the second century B.C. Evidence of an ancient sanctuary have also been detected in the vicinity.
A villa attributed to Cnaeus Pompeius.

S. Passera is a Christian church on the Tiber river in Rome, opposite the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls. The current church dates to the ninth century and incorporated the remains of a Roman tomb. The church is traditionally connected to a community of local miners.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 Il Torraccio
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Tomba di Marco Plauzio Lucano
An imperial Roman tomb of Publius Vibius Marianus, erroneously identified as the Tomba di Nerone (Tomb of Nero) by G. B. Piranesi.
A circular mausoleum dating to the Late Republican period along the Via Praenestina.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 S. Martino
The Ponte Salario is a Medieval bridge with Roman origins. It is located at the point where the Via Salaria crosses the Anio, about 3 km north of the Colline Gate.

The Papal Basilica of Saint Lawrence outside the Walls (Basilica Papale di San Lorenzo fuori le Mura) is one of the Seven Pilgrim Churches of Rome. The basilica serves as the shrine and tomb dedicated to Saint Lawrence and its earliest phases likely belong to the fourth century AD.
The modern toponym Tor Marancia is claimed to derive from the Praedium Amaranthianus, a villa belonging to the second-century A.D. freedman Amaranthus.
The Mausoleum of the Plautii dates to the first century B.C. It is located near Ponte Lucano at Tibur.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Settebagni
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 E2 S. Clemens

A Christian catacomb within an ancient quarry on the Via Salaria that was in use from the second until the fourth centuries AD. The Catacomb of Priscilla was likely named for Priscilla, a member of the gens Acilia, and contains the oldest known Marian painting (third century AD).
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 Pietra Papa
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 S. Sinforosa
The so-called "Il Torraccio (1)" is the cement core of a Roman tomb located at the twelfth milestone of the Via Appia Nuova, on the left side.

A villa located near the sanctuary of Madonna di Quintiliolo (Tivoli) that is traditionally associated with Quintilius Varus. The remains of the basis villae may date as early as the third century B.C.
A coastal Roman villa that is succeeded by a Medieval coastal tower.

Sublanuvium was an ancient station (statio) along the Via Appia, located between Aricia and Ad Sponsas. While its precise location is unknown, the site is located at the twentieth milestone of the Appia.

Saxa Rubra (modern Grottarossa) is the name of a road station on the Via Flaminia nine Roman miles from the center of ancient Rome. It was at Saxa Rubra that Constantine I defeated Maxentius in A.D. 312.
The basilica and catacombs of S. Alessandro are located at the seventh milestone of the Via Nomentana.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 S. Antonio

An ancient settlement on the right bank of the river Astura, Satricum has a mixed heritage of Latins and Volscians. In 499 B.C. Satricum was a member of the Latin League, but was under Volscian control in 488 B.C. The site is noted for its sanctuary of Mater Matuta.
A Final Bronze Age settlement of four to five hectares in South Etruria.
A station on the Via Cassia attested in an inscription dated to A.D. 379-383.
A Roman tomb near Albano Laziale connected in tradition with the story of the contest between the Horatii and Curiatii.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C4 Torre Caldara
S. Sebastianus (San Sebastiano fuori le mura) is a Christian basilica outside the walls of Rome; the earliest phase belongs to the fourth century AD.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Pietralata
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 S. Cesareo
A large catacomb on the Via Appia south of Rome notable especially for its so-called 'Crypt of the Popes'. The catacomb covers approximately 15 hectares.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C4 Torre del Monumento
A convent founded within the area of the Villa Neronis.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B3 Piscina Torta
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Prati Fiscali
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 S. Felicita
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 S. Agata

The tomb C. Maenius Bassus is located along the Via Valeria. This podium tomb with superstructure is dated to either the reign of Caius or that of Claudius. Epigraphic evidence mentions that C. Maenius C. f. Cam. Bassus was an Augustalis, an aedile, and praefectus fabrum.
At Solforata along the Via Ardeatina activity related to the extraction of sulfur has been identified.
The Tomb of Annia Regilla (vix. A.D. 125-160), the wife of Herodes Atticus. The tomb is also erroneously known as the "Temple of the God Rediculum" and was used in the Middle Ages as a hay barn.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D1 S. Vincenzo

A Roman villa near the line of the Aqua Claudia located in the modern Via del Quadraro. The villa is dated to the first century B.C. or first century A.D. Following remodelling in the third century, the villa's occupation ends in the fourth century.
A suburban villa built by Sextus Quintilius Maximus and Sextus Quintilius Condianus (consuls in A.D. 151).
A Christian catacomb along the Via Flaminia dedicated to S. Valentino.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Scalzacane

A titular church on the Via Nomentana, S. Agnese houses the remains of the eponymous saint. The present church was built by Pope Honorius I in the seventh century AD, on the site of a fourth century basilica built by Constantine I.
S. Ermete is the site of a Paleochristian basilica and catacomb; the catacombs are also referred to as the Catacombs of Bassilla, and both names occur in the documentary sources.

Prima Porta, located to the north of Rome, allegedly derives its modern name from the remains of a Roman aqueduct whose presence signaled to travelers on the Via Flaminia that they had reached Rome. The site is best known for an Imperial villa that belonged to the family of Livia Drusilla.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 S. Rufina
An ancient settlement, located at modern Subiaco in Italy, Sublaqueum was located in the territory of the Aequi that was annexed by Rome in 304 B.C.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C3 Torre del Padiglione
A Sabine town, 30 km east-north-east of Rome, Tibur was the seat of the Tiburtine Sibyl.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 S. Carlo
Ancient tuff quarries and a bridge at Salone on the Anio River.
A Roman tomb along the Via Appia that is traditionally believed to be that of Publius Septimius Geta, the younger son of Septimius Severus.
The sanctuary of the god Robigus, located at the sixth mile of the Via Cassia. The Romans celebrated the festival of Robigalia on 25 April.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B1 S. Maria di Galeria
A large, suburban villa complex on the Via Tuscolana. The villa was in use from the reign of Antoninus Pius until the fourth century A.D.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Il Tondo
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B3 Tor Paterno

The Basilica of St. Peter in Vatican City is currently a Renaissance edifice standing on the site of Old St. Peter's Basilica, a church built by Constantine I between AD 319 and 333. The holy site is located on the Mons Vaticanus in connection with the purported site of the burial of the Christian Saint Peter.
Basilica Papale di San Pietro in Vaticano

The so-called villa of Pliny the Younger, also known as the Villa della Palombara. The villa's first phases date to the Iulio-Claudian period. It continues in use, and continues to undergo modifications, through the second century A.D.
The great ancient maritime port of Rome, located on the right-hand bank of the Tiber River.
Area Archeologica del Porto di Traiano
A catacomb connected with the Christian Saint Hippolytus of Rome along the Via Tiburtina.

An ancient city of central Italy, the eighth and seventh century B.C. origins of which demonstrate high-level trade contact with the Eastern Mediterranean world. The city withdrew from the Latin League (499 B.C.) and opposed Rome in the Latin war; Cincinnatus eventually subdued Praeneste. Sulla founded a new colony there in the first century B.C.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D3 Pometia

One of Rome's four major papal basilicae, S. Paulus was founded by Constantine I in the early fourth century A.D. and expanded by Valentinian I in the 370s. The basilica, with many renovations, repairs, and improvements, stood until the 19th century, when it was destroyed in a fire. The reconstructed basilica only generally resembles the original structure.
Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls
Basilica Papale di San Paolo fuori le Mura
Sacer Mons is a hill on the banks of the Anio River and is connected, traditionally, with the episode of the secession of the Roman plebs of 494 BC.

A Roman tomb, known as the Torraccia dell’Inviolata. This tomb has a cruciform plan that is inscribed within a circular structure. Based on masonry techniques the tomb dates to the later first or second century.
A Volscian settlement of the fifth century B.C. that became a Latin colony in 382 B.C.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Tor Angela

The church of Saints Marcellinus and Peter is a Roman Catholic church located on the Via Merulana in Rome. Pope Siricius built the original church in the fourth century A.D., close to the catacombs of Marcellinus and Peter. The relics of the saints were deposited in the church in 1256.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Ponte di Tuscolo
The capital of the Roman Republic and Empire.
A city of Latium Adjectum established as a Latin colony ca. 494 B.C.

A tomb on the Via Appia south of Rome belonging to Caecilia Metella, a daughter of Metellus Creticus. She was born ca. 100 BC. In 1303 the tomb was incorporated into the Castrum Caetani, serving as the main tower of the fortification.
Located in Messenia, Nichoria was a site with important Bronze Age and Iron Age phases.
A small temple of Artemis Aristoboule ("of best deliberation") erected by Themistokles
A Roman villa located on via Lemonia in Rome's suburbium attributed to Quintus Servilius Pudens.
An Iron Age settlement in Latium.

An Iron Age settlement and necropolis located in the Monti Lepini near the abbey of Valvisciolo, characterized by polygonal masonry terrace walls. While the ancient name of the site is unknown, various proposals have been raised, including Sulmo (Savignoni, Mengarelli) and Pometia (Ogilvie). The settlement corresponds to the Latial II B phase and occupation ends ca. the late sixth century B.C.
Varia (modern Vicovaro) was a settlement of the Sabines.

The Villa Aldobrandini is located on the outskirts of Frascati. The current villa of the site was built in 1550 by a Vatican prelate named Alessandro Rufini. Subsequently, Pope Clement VIII gave the villa to his nephew Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini in 1598. The Papal villa and gardens occupy the site of a Roman terrace villa.
A large imperial Roman villa known from letters of Marcus Aurelius.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Via delle Piagge
A Latin federal sanctuary at Lavinium, consisting of a series of altars that range in date from the sixth to the second century BC and a sacred site (or heroon) connected with the hero Aeneas.
A large villa complex that was built sometime in the first century B.C.E. and remained in use until at least the third century C.E.
Tusculum was a Latin city of the Alban Hills in central Italy. After 381 B.C., Tusculum became the first "municipium cum suffragio".

The church of San Pancrazio was founded in the sixth century A.D. by Pope Symmachus. It stands beyond the Porta San Pancrazio on the Ianiculum. Below the church is a massive catacomb referred to as S. Pancrazio or Ottavilla.
The so-called Villa of Vibius Varus is located south of the Villa Adriana at Tivoli. The site has three architectural phases stretching from the first century BCE to the fourth century CE
Villa Domitiani, a large imperial villa near the Alban Lake, now the site of the Papal retreat at Castel Gandolfo.
A Jewish catacomb discovered in 1919 on the grounds of the Villa Torlonia park in Rome.
A complex on the Via Appia constructed by Maxentius in the early fourth century A.D.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Valerio Messala Corvino
A statio at the point where the Via Appia crosses the Via Ninfina.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 Villa Esmeade
The Villa Neronis was a rural villa of the emperor Nero, likely built early in his reign (perhaps before AD 60).
The Villa of Hadrian (Villa Adriana in Italian) is a sprawling archaeological complex at Tivoli, Italy. The villa complex was designed and used by the emperor Hadrian in the second century A.D.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B3 Troia?
A settlement at the third milestone of the Via Ostiensis.
An important city of South Etruria located north-northwest of Rome, Veii was eventually sacked by the Romans in 396 B.C. The ancient city covered some 180 ha.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Torre S. Angelo
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D3 Torre Sessano

Velitrae (modern Velletri) was an ancient Volscian settlement. In the Roman Republican period, Velitrae was attacked by Marcus Furius Camillus (379 B.C.) and again by Cincinnatus (377 B.C.); the Romans controlled the site by 365 B.C. The gens Octavia hailed from the city and a youthful Octavian spent time there.

The Vicus Augustanus Laurentium is an ancient settlement in coastal Latium located between the shore and the Via Severiana. The site was first described by Rodolfo Lanciani in 1903. The British School at Rome carried out excavations in the 1980s.
Two coastal villas (villae maritimae) discovered in 2003 and 2004, respectively.
Tell Beydar (ancient Nabada) is an archaeological site in NE Syria that was first settled ca. 2600 BC.
Settlement and industrial site in southern Cyprus dated to the Early and Middle Bronze Ages.
A temple of the Doric order that was built at Akragas ca. 450 BCE.
Plutarch describes a villa owned by Lucullus near Tusculum.

An ancient Latin city located on the line of the Republican Via Praenestina connecting Rome to Praeneste. Gabii is allied to Rome from an early date and flourished during the archaic period, declining by the time of Augustus.
At Forte Tiburtina the remains of a Roman villa located on the northern edge of the Parco della Serenissima in the eastern suburbium of the city of Rome.

Monte del Grano is a popular name that was assigned to a mausoleum once thought to belong to Alexander Severus, although that assignation is no longer supported. The archaeological remains are now part of the Parco XVII Aprile 1944.
An important Latial sanctuary of Iuppiter located on Mons Albanus (modern Monte Cavo).

The Latin town of Nomentum and Rome were linked by means of the Via Nomentana. In Livy's history the town, a member of the Latin League, is captured by Lucius Tarquinius Priscus. Nomentum was one of a number of towns captured by Tarquinius. The Romans granted the town civitas sine suffragio after 338 B.C.

John Ward-Perkins identified the archaeological site at Fosso della Crescenza during the South Etruria Survey. Excavations of a Iulio-Claudian mausoleum were undertaken in 1962. Additional excavation revealed portions of the Via Veientana. Post-excavation work did not occur until the 1980s, by which time Fentress 1983 notes that the archaeological landscape had been largely eradicated by the burgeoning growth of suburban Rome.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 A2 Ladispoli
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D3 Crepaddosso

Originally a member of the Latin League, the city of Labicum was taken by the Romans ca. 418 B.C. By the time of Augustus, the site was almost certainly deserted and its precise location remains debated today.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Colle Tasso
The archaeological remains of a Roman villa on the hill of San Cesareo are speculatively identified as belonging to the gens Octavia, according to Della Portella 2004 op. cit.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Frascati
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 Magliana Vecchia
Norba, located in the Monti Lepini, was a member of the Latin League (ca. 499 B.C.) and became a Latin colony ca. 492 B.C. The city was destroyed in the early first century B.C.
An extensive second and third century A.D. necropolis located between the city of Ostia and Portus.
A Latin center in the Monti Lepini that was already a Roman municipium by 211 B.C.
A Renaissance villa (Villa Mondragone) was built atop the platform of a Roman villa dating to the first century B.C.
A Roman villa located at Acquatraversa on the Via Cassia that is frequently attributed to Lucius Verus.
Munazio Planco, the so-called Villa of Munatius Plancus and villa on Via delle Piagge.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Grotta di Paris
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Montioni
A plaform villa at Colle Nocello.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C1 Lamnae/Ad Lam(i)nas

An ancient town of Latium located at the headwaters of the Allia river, very close to the territory of the Sabines, Crustumerium figures in Rome's early history. The Romans conquered the site in 500 B.C. and formed the tribus Crustumina or Clustumina in 471 B.C.
An ancient town on the Via Aurelia.
A fourth century A.D. catacomb along the via Salaria at Rome.
Ficulea was an ancient city of Latium situated between Rome and Nomentum.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Montedoro
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 Monte dell'Oro
Fidenae was an ancient city of Latium.
A fortified site on the Via Appia dating to the Republican period.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Lolli Paolini

The quarries at Grotta Oscura were an important source of high-quality tuff located in the territory of Veii. This was the "tuffo giallo della via Tiberina" that was used at Rome from the Archaic period onward.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Laghetto di Colonna
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Colle Rosa

The hill of Monteverde, a part of the Ianiculum hill to the west of the Tiber river, was a source of a brown, lithoid tuff (tufo di Monteverde) that was quarried for use as a building material from the second century BC.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Pedum?

The site of a Roman villa situated on two terraces. The modern toponym "Grotta Papale" derives from a partially subterranean apsidal nymphaeum. The villa was extensive, covering some 23,000 square meters and has both a late republican and an imperial phase.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Muraccio dell’Omo

The Arval Brethren cultivated the cult of the Dea Dia. Remains of this Augustan era temple, located at La Tavernaccia restaurant in the Magliana vecchia neighborhood of Rome, are subterranean and not open to the public.

Grottarossa is located at the intersection of key roadways in northern suburbium of Rome, lying along the Via Flaminia as well as at the point where the Via Veientana separated from the Via Cassia and thereby connected Rome with Veii. There is archaeological evidence for tombs, both built tombs and rock-cut tombs in the exposed tuff escarpments, as well as villas.
A Roman tomb of the second or third century CE.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D3 Colle Medico
The site of a major Iron Age necropolis (Latial chronology) composed of over 600 burials.
A large Christian basilica discovered in 1976 several hundred meters southeast of the Porta Laurentina of Ostia. The original phase dates to the end of the fourth century A.D.

An Etruscan and Roman site lying 4 km to the west of Caere along the monumental road leading to Pyrgi. Until the early 1960s, the site was known for the monumental tumulus that Mengarelli had excavated in the 1920s. Subsequent excavation revealed other evidence, including an elite compound that served as a sanctuary.
A third century A.D. villa complex along the Via Praenestina connected with Gordian I, Gordian II, and Gordian III.
An ancient city of Latium on the Numicus River that was founded, according to Virgil, by Aeneas.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Grotta del Mortale

An ancient city of Latium that was said to have been conquered by Ancus Marcius, Ficana was located near the eleventh mile of the Via Ostiensis. Excavation at the site has produced important evidence for the urban center beginning from the eighth century BC. Pliny the Elder mentions Ficana as one of the lost cities of Latium.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Pianelle
Monteroni, near Ladispoli, is the site of an Etruscan necropolis.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 Naumachia
The port city of ancient Rome located at the mouth of the river Tiber.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Colle Monitola

Lanuvium was an important city of Latium located south of the Alban Hills. After opposing Rome at the battle of Aricia (504 B.C.) and Lake Regillus (496 B.C.), Lanuvium was captured by the Romans in 338 B.C.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Grottaferrata
A site sacred to Diana near Lake Nemi, comprised of a Tuscan-style sanctuary and a sacred grove.

The Domus Marmeniae is a villa located on the Via Appia near the fourth milestone. The villa grounds hosted a pagan necropolis and tradition holds that the matrona, Marmenia, relocated the body of St. Urban to a mausoleum built on the grounds.
A sanctuary dedicated to Fortuna Muliebris along the Via Latina. Tradition holds that it was dedicated in 487 B.C.
An ancient town of Etruria, Fregenae was located between Alsium and the mouth of the river Tiber.
An ancient town of Latium connected with the origins of Servius Tullius.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Inviolata
Colle Vitriano is the site of a Roman villa supported on two artificial terraces that utilize megalithic walling in the polygonal masonry technique as well as caementicium.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Opimiano
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C4 Nettuno
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 Ospedale di S. Camillo
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 La Colombella
A temple located at the fourth mile of the Via Appia.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Corzano
An ancient road station on the Via Appia located 69 km southeast of Rome.
Marina di S. Nicola is located close to Alsium.
The Tomb of Arellia Tertulla, daughter of Numerius and wife of Veius Fronto.

A Bronze Age settlement on the island of Lemnos, Poliochne pre-dates Troy I and shows influence from the Greek mainland during Early Helladic II (ca. 2500 BC). Mycenaean horizons have also been identified.
A fifth century B.C. Doric temple, the so-called Temple of Hera II is also sometimes referred to as the Temple of Neptune.

Collatia was an ancient city of Latium located between Gabii and the Anio Rover. A colony of Alba Longa, Collatia was one of the most ancient cities of Latium. Subjugated by Rome under the Tarquins, Collatia would decline during the Republican period and numbers among the lost Latin cities by the accounting of Pliny the Elder.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Case Nuove 2
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C3 Campo del Fico

Antemnae is an ancient Latin settlement located north of Rome near the point where the Anio and Tiber rivers intersect. Connected with Rome's early history, Antemnae was involved in episodes such as the 'Rape of the Sabine Women' and Romulus is said to have celebrated a triumph over the Antemnates in 752 BC.
A major Roman necropolis and catacomb along the Via Nomentana.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Castel Madama
Ad Sponsas was a road station on the Via Appia.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Cabum?
Ad Statuas was a road station on the Via Labicana located east of Rome.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B3 Castelporziano
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Cinecittà

Antium ranked as one of the most important and most powerful centers of Latium and was captured by Rome at the close of the Latin War in the fourth century B.C. Imperial Antium was well known for its number of coastal villas.
A Christian catacomb originally containing the tombs of Pope Callixtus I and Pope Julius I, along with that of the eponymous Saint Calepodius.

Colle Gentile is a naturally defensible hill with good visibility located in the environs of Norba. While the site has not been scientifically excavated, it has been surveyed. The Groningen Institute of Archaeology identified traces of polygonal masonry fortification walls as well as surface ceramics that indicate settlement activity associated with Archaic and Republican phases. Imperial period activity is absent.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Case Nuove 1
Aefula was an ancient settlement of Latium that had disappeared by the time of Pliny the Elder, although the cult of Bona Dea there continued to flourish.
Castel Savello takes its name from a fifteenth-century fortress of the Savelli family at Albano Laziale. Funerary evidence associated with the Latial culture has been documented here.

The road station of Ad Decimum corresponds with the archaeological area of Castel di Decima where archaeological excavations in the 1970s identified the remains of a settlement covering some 11 hectares that dates to the eighth through sixth centuries BCE. Excavations revealed not only habitation evidence but also several hundred tombs.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Bel Poggio
A villa at the seventh mile of the Via Latina.
The Villa dei Centroni, located on the modern via Anagnina, lay at the ninth mile of the ancient via Latina. It dates from the first century B.C. onward.
The church and convent "I Cappuccini" in Frascati was the site of a Roman villa.
Alsium served as a port for Caere, together with Fregenae.
The Roman temple dedicated to Ceres and Faustina received patronage from Herodes Atticus. Its remains were eventually repurposed in the construction of the church of Sant'Urbano.
The site of a villa located between Frascati and Monte Porzio Catone. It is associated with Matidia Augusta on account of an inscribed fistula discovered there in 1888.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Casale del Cavaliere
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Albuccione
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Ad Decimum
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Ad Nonum
Castra Albana was a permanent, fortified camp of the Legio II Parthica constructed during the Severan period.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Ciciliano
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Bruto e Pisoni
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Ad Nonum (1)
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D3 Artena
A Roman tomb that supports a Medieval farmhouse (casale) at the sixth mile of the Via Appia. The tomb originally dates ca. 30 BC; it was a large, circular tomb with a diameter of approximately 35 m.
A Latin settlement that became a Roman municipium.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Cervara 1

The toponym 'Ad Duas Lauros' refers to a large imperial property at the third mile of the Via Labicana and today comprising the archaeological park of Centocelle. The site is mentioned in the Liber Pontificalis as that of a large imperial villa in which Helena, mother of Constantine I, lived. Archaeological work conducted in the late 1990s identified the remains of substantial Republican-period villas in the same area, with evidence of both elite dwellings and viticulture. The villas identified are the Villa della Piscina and the Villa Ad Duas Lauros.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Il Barco
A small site in Latium (?1.2 hectares) that may have been fortified as early as the eighth century BCE.

A villa located at the eighth mile of the ancient Via Latina. The villa was first built in the first century B.C. and continued in use until the fourth century. During its life span there were several phases of architectural modification and expansion.

Alba Longa, located in the Alban Hills southeast of Rome, was the chief city and founder of the Latin League. Conflict with Rome caused Alba's destruction in the seventh century B.C. The legendary history of Romulus and Remus connects them to the royal lineage of the city. The ancient city is probably to be located at and around the site of modern Castel Gandolfo.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Casale Martellona
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Capannacce
Anagnia was a Hernican town that sided with Rome against the Volscians and later became civitas sine suffragio. By Cicero's time it received the status of municipium.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 A2 Baebiana
Ad Gallinas Albas refers to a location along the Via Flaminia.
An ancient settlement of Latium located in the territory of the Aequi.
In the vicinity of Tor Cervara are anio tuff (tufo d'Aniene) quarries.
An ancient town on the Via Clodia.
The so-called "Torraccio della Cecchina" is a Roman funereal monument dating to the second century A.D. It is located at the ninth kilometer of the modern Via Nomentana.
Aricia is an ancient Latin settlement and a member of the Latin League.
Ad Pictas is a road station east of Rome, known mostly for its role in Sulla's march on Rome in 88 B.C. The precise location of the statio continues to be debated.
A statio in Latium located at the intersection of the Via Latina and the Via Labicana, near the modern Valmontone.
A town of ancient Latium along the line of the Via Appia, Bovillae is traditionally considered to be a colony of Alba Longa and was one of the thirty cities of the Latin League.
Caere (also known as Cisra or Cerveteri) was a major Etruscan polis located ca. 50 km north-northwest of Rome in southern Etruria.
Ad Turres was located on the Via Aurelia some 10 miles from Lorium and 12 miles from Pyrgi.
T. Ashby notes the presence of a villa platform to the west of the "upper Casale Vitriano". This platform seems to be a terrace at least 34 m in length.
Buon Riposo is a small, fortified settlement covering some 2 hectares. Its fortifications date to the seventh century BCE or later.
A settlement along the Via Laurentina that has yielded significant evidence for protohistoric occupation, including funereal evidence of the eighth and seventh centuries B.C.
Ad Quintanas is the name of a road station on the Via Labicana.
Ardea was an ancient settlement of the Rutuli in Latium.
The so-called 'Villa of the Antonines', located near Genzano di Roma in the Alban Hills, lies just south of the Via Appia between the road's 18th and 19th milestones.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 A2 Castel Campanile

A villa in Tibur that has been incorrectly linked to Gaius Cassius Longinus. In the eighteenth century, the site produced a cache of Egyptianizing sculpture that likely dates to the reign of Hadrian and is now held in the Vatican Museums.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D3 Civitana

Ashby describes a rich archaeological landscape that once included the remains of Roman-period tombs and villas, the latter appointed with mosaics. The modern toponym "Case Rosse" is said to derive from a well-preserved Roman tomb executed in brick that was purposefully destroyed in 1824.
Cicero describes the villa of Publius Clodius Pulcher as being located at the thirteenth mile of the Via Appia near Bovillae.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D3 Le Castella
An imperial villa of the Trajanic and Hadrianic periods located on the Altipiani di Arcinazzo.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 Ad Sextum
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 B2 Acquafredda
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C3 Buglioncino
Located in the Anio river valley to the south of Subiaco, Afilae was a municipium that was likely assigned to the tribus Aniensis.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D3 Casali

Campoverde (Lazio) lies some 60 km south of Rome. In 1977-1978 a quantity of votive material was recovered from a body of water known as the "Laghetto del Monsignore". This spring-fed body of water was interpreted as an open-air votive depository.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 C2 Annunziatella
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 43 D2 Adriano

The Temple of Athena Pallenis was built in the mid-6th century BC and rebuilt on a larger scale in the late 5th century BC. In myth, the location was the site of King Eurystheus' tomb and Theseus' victory over the Pallantidai. In 546 BC, it was the site of the battle by which Peisistratos finally established his tyranny. At the end of the 1st century BC, the structure was disassembled and rebuilt in the Agora of Athens as the Temple of Ares.

A classical/hellenistic temple located in the likely territory of Acarnanian Alyzeia. The temple site lies over 6km southeast from the ancient walled city (about a kilometer south of modern Paliovarka, Greece) at a site known in modern times as Drymonas Archontochoriou. It is perched on rising ground with a view westward to the channel and the island of Karnos (modern Kalamos). Inscriptions have been recovered from the site, and an unlooted portion of a votive deposit was scientifically excavated in the 1990s.

Khirbet Qeiyafa, also known as Elah Fortress, is an Iron Age fortress site located about 40 kilometers southwest of Jerusalem, overlooking the Elah Valley. The site was likely constructed in the late eleventh century BCE and destroyed or abandoned in the mid- to late tenth century BCE.

From the second half of the third millennium BC until 614 BC, there was a temple in Assur dedicated to the city’s tutelary deity Aššur. The temple was excavated by W. Andrae in 1903–05 and 1909–12. The earliest and latest textual records for construction work on Aššur’s temple date respectively to the time of Šalim-aḫum, an early old Assyrian king, and the reign of Ashurbanipal (668–631 BC), Assyria’s last great king. According to the Middle Assyrian king Shalmaneser I (1263–1234 BC) and the Neo-Assyrian ruler Esarhaddon (680–669 BC), Ušpia, a tribal ancestor of the Old Assyrian king Šamšī-Adad I (ca. 1808–1776 BC), was the building’s founder. In 614 BC, when the city was captured by the Medes, the temple was destroyed.

The temple of the goddess Šarrat-Larsa, Emekiliburur (“House which Gathers All the Me’s”), was located in the Kullab district of Babylon, in the eastern half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of four temples in that part of Babylon.

The temple of the god Sîn, Ekišnugal (“House of the Great Light”), was located in the Kullab district of Babylon, in the eastern half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of four temples in that part of Babylon. The temple is mentioned in Old Babylonian Period texts and was (re)built by the Old Babylonian king Abī-ēšuh (r. ca. 1711–1684 BC) and the Neo-Babylonian ruler Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 604–562 BC). The temple survived into the Hellenistic Period.

Hurkum (Dilkaya) is a modern village situated on the southern shore of Lake Van in the Southeast of Turkey near Ishanikom. In its church, a re-used column base with an inscription of the Urartian king Minua, son of Išpuini (9th / 8th century BCE) was found which reports the building of a banquet hall (CTU A 5-65C). Two other column bases with the same inscription have been found in a private house near the historic center of Van (CTU A 5-65A) and in a church of the monastery of Warrak Kilisa or Yedikilise (CTU A 5-65B).

The temple of the goddess Ninmah/Bēlet-ilī, Emah (“Exalated House”), was located in the Ka-dingirra district (modern Kasr) of Babylon. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, this was one of four temples in that part of the city, which was located in the northern part of the eastern half of Babylon. Emah was rebuilt by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal (r. 668–ca. 631 BC) and the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 604–562 BC).

The temple of the god Šara, Ebursasa (“House of Beautiful Jars”), was located in the Bāb-Lugalerra district of Babylon, in the western half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of three temples in that part of Babylon.

The temple of the goddess Bēlet-Ninūa, Egišhurankia (“House of the Ordinances of Heaven and Underworld”), was located in the Bāb-Lugalerra district of Babylon, in the western half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of three temples in that part of Babylon. Egišhurankia seems to have been located near Imgur-Enlil, along the northern wall.

A coastal station or anchorage and associated settlement that scholars identify with the modern Khawr/Khor Ghurayrah on Yemen's Ra’s Shaykh Sa‘īd headland in the Bab al-Mandab Strait. This small bay is almost closed by sand and coral reefs today. The precise location of the ancient settlement is not known.

A small, fortified town that served as an outpost for the Ḥaḑramawt kingdom from the first to seventh centuries. The archaeological site and its surrounding landscape are known by the modern name Khor Rori, and the town is tentatively identified as Ptolemy's Abyssapolis, and the port of Moscha Limen of the Periplus Maris Erythraei.

Tumulus covering a rich Celtic burial of ca. 530 BC.

An unnamed settlement close to the modern village of Casian is also not far from the rock inscriptions from the Șeremet forest. The rock inscriptions mention the limits of the community of the Kasians and their caves. A house from the Roman period and some coins were found here. The relation between the settlement and the toponym Kasiana or Kasianon is not clear, because of the position of the inscriptions.
Ancient site on the promontory of Strophilas, Andros. Archaeological evidence of a town from Late Neolithic to Early Cycladic (4500-3300 BC).

Sippar-Amnanum (modern Tell ed-Der; also referred to as Sippar-Annunītu) was a small city located 6 km northeast of Sippar and 63 km north of Babylon. The goddess Annunītu was the patron deity of this sister city of Sippar and Eulmaš was its principal temple. An archive of ca. 2,000 cuneiform tablets dating the the reigns of several kings of the First Dynasty of Babylon were excavated in the house of Ur-Utu, the chief lamentation-priest of the goddess Annunītu. From several inscriptions of Nabonidus (r. 555–539 BC), Babylon’s last native king, it is certain that Sippar-Amnanum (which he refers to as Sippar-Annunītu) was still occupied and its cult was still in use in the sixth century BC, although it had been (partially) destroyed by the seventh-century-BC Assyrian king Sennacherib (r. 704–681 BC).
Terrace and altar of M. Nonius Balbus

Marcus Nonius Balbus of Nuceria was an important civic patron of Herculaneum. Balbus was a praetor and proconsul of Crete and Cyrene and served as tribune of the plebs in 32 B.C. This architectural complex near the Suburban Baths included the terrace as well as an honorific statue and altar.
A Neolithic site and cemetery on Keos.
A Roman villa commonly associated with Q. Voconius Pollio that was excavated in the nineteenth century.

Now lost, the so-called "Isis Tomb" was excavated at Vulci in the 19th century. Based on finds evidence, the tomb is traditionally dated ca. 625 to 550 B.C. Its traditionally assigned name is likely a misnomer, based on a contemporary identification of a bronze bust as representing the Egyptian goddess Isis. The subsequent back-filling of the tomb and uncareful recording at the time have caused the tomb's location to be lost to us.
A Roman auxiliary fort in Scotland guarding the road from Trimontium to Castledykes.

The mastaba-style tomb of Ptahshepses, vizier to the Fifth Dynasty Pharaoh Nyuserre Ini. Following the intial elite burials in the Old Kingdom, the mastaba became a funerary site for new burials during the Late Period.
A town mentioned in Neo-Assyrian sources; the modern site is T. Ǧāmā.
A major Late Bronze Age city in the Amuq River Valley, inhabited during the Second Millennium BCE until about the 12th century BCE.

The Assyrian king Adad-nārārī III (r. 810-783 BC) constructed a palace for himself at Kalhu (biblical Calah, modern Nimrud). This royal residence, whose walls were covered with white plaster and painted with geometric and floral motifs, was built immediately to the south of the palace of his great-grandfather Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883–859 BC).
Unnamed settlement near Teniet Ennasr, Algeria

Remains of an ancient settlement of Roman date, recorded by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas). The location should lie within 2 km of the BAtlas coordinates: a point near the modern CW 43 road just to the northeast of Teniet Ennasr in the Algerian wilaya of Bordj Bou Arreridj.
A Roman auxiliary fort located at Drumlanrig in Scotland.

A major, but relatively short-lived, fortified site in the Zagros mountains of modern Iraqi Kurdistan comprising two settlement loci within a large fortified area. Remains include stone foundations for mudbrick fortification walls and buildings, a stone-cut stairway, and two rock-reliefs depicting an unnamed ruler in elaborate costume. The complex has some evidence for reoccupation in Sasanian, Islamic and modern times.

The so-called "Areni-1 cave complex" is an archaeological site located near the Areni village in southern Armenia along the Arpa River. The site shows evidence for both ritual and occupational activity in the late Chalcolithic to Early Bronze Age.
A place from the TAVO Index
Theatrum Marcelli (Theater of Marcellus) is an ancient Roman theater in the Circus Flaminius. Augustus completed its construction and dedicated it in 12 BC.

Tarbiṣu, now modern Sherif Khan, was an Assyrian city located about 5 kilometers north of Nineveh. It was the principal cult center of the god Nergal in Assyria. Starting in the 8th and 7th centuries B.C., Tarbiṣu was a royal city and one of the primary residences of the Assyrian crown prince, who was trained in the art of kingship in the palace built there.
The Castillo de Cote was built toward the end of the 13th century on the orders of Alfonso X.
A small, underground tomb-like structure located in the agora of Paestum, thought to be either a shrine or a heroon.
Settlement site near Abdul Hosein village in Luristan, Iran dated to the Neolithic period. The site was occupied by non-sedentary people who left behind no structures besides a wall.
Located to the west of Hippo Regius (modern Annaba in Algeria).

A major paleochristian, then Byzantine, church in Istanbul; subsequently an Islamic mosque, and today a museum.

Located at modern Floga in the town of Paros, this residential structure, dating to the 5th/4th centuries BCE, underwent a number of subsequent modifications and took on the additional role of a sculpture workshop in the Hellenistic period.

The so-called Temple of Augustus et Livia dates ca. 10 B.C. and was originally dedicated to Roma and Augustus. The temple was located on the ancient forum of the city. By the fifth century the temple had become a Christian church. It was extensively restored in the nineteenth century.

The archaeological area of Costia dei Lippi is located near the contemporary cemetery of Vetulonia. Excavations in this area began in the 1960s and revealed a series of stone walls built in a squared technique, as well as a system of terraces and a paved road. The area has been interpreted as a domestic quarter dating ca. the third to the first century BCE.
An Old Kingdom cemetery located in the Dakhla Oasis, Balat, Egypt, that contains the tombs of royal officials who governed the area of the oasis.
The Yeavering Bell is a twin-peaked hill fort in Northumberland, England, that forms part of the Cheviot Hills.

Located outside the city walls of Pergamon, this temple, according to an inscription (OGIS 273-9), was supposedly the site of a victory of Attalos I over the Tolistogi, Galatians, and Antiochus Hierax. It was likely later destroyed by Philip V.
An ancient place, cited: BAtlas 31 B4 no. 1 (mausoleum)

Quintus Lollius Urbicus served as a governor of Britannia between 139 and 142. His career is detailed on a pair of inscriptions from his hometown of Tiddis. His mausoleum is located a few kilometers north of Tiddis.

The Ajanta Caves are among the earliest Buddhist cave monuments and date from the second and first centuries B.C. During the Gupta period (fifth and sixth centuries A.D.), additional decorated caves were added to the group.
Site of extensive Roman occupation and possible Claudio-Neronian military base where Ermine Street crosses the river Humber, opposite the fort at Petuaria (Brough-on-Humber).
Archaeological site on the Yarkon River in modern Tel Aviv, identified as a Philistine city inhabited during the 12th and 11th centuries BCE.
A megalithic complex located near Guadalupe, Portgual, dating to the Early Neolithic period.

The archaeological site of Mehrgarh covers an area of some 250 ha. It is located in the Kachi plain (Balochistan, Pakistan) near the Bolan Pass. The Neolithic-period site consists of numerous archaeological mounds.

Maidanetske, Ukraine, is the site of two separate Neolithic to Chalcolithic settlements associated with the Cucuteni-Trypillian culture. A 2-hectare settlement dating ca. 5000 BCE lies on the outskirts of Maidanetske, Ukraine while another, larger settlement (ca. 3700 BCE) was found west of Maidanetske on the left bank of the Tal'ianki River.
The larger of the two mounds that make up the Tall-e Bakun site.
A Medieval settlement where numerous important Etruscan tombs have been excavated.
A villa, vicus, and necropolis site in modern Puglia, Italy, located near the modern city of Gravina. The site was active from the first to fourth centuries CE.
A major Early Bronze Age necropolis on Syros, Chalandriani contains tombs related to the Keros-Syros culture of the Early Cycladic II period.

The fortified settlement of Kastri near Chalandriani on the Cycladic island of Syros is an important Early Cycladic II site. This fortified hill-top settlement is a very early example of a site in the Aegean with a fortification wall reinforced by means of stone bastions.

This ornately-decorated, elevated building might have been the residence of Sammu-ramat (the legendary Semiramis) in the palace of her son Adad-nārārī III (r. 810-783 BC) at Kalhu (biblical Calah, modern Nimrud). Because these rooms were built noticeably higher than the surrounding area, its first excavator Austen Henry Layard believed that he had uncovered part of an upper floor of an Assyrian palace and, therefore, referred to this area as the “Upper Chambers.”
Zetis was an ancient city of Carmania, although its location can no longer be determined.
A city founded by Alexander the Great, perhaps in 324 B.C., which might be identical with the later Gulashkird/Golashkerd/Valashgird in Kerman Province of Iran.
A Spanish city located in Andalusia that once belonged to the kingdom of Alfonso X. It is now known as Jaén.
Surviving colonnade of the imperial temple at Mérida
Burial area in the northwestern portion of the Giza Necropolis containing burials dated to the Fourth-Fifth Dynasties.

A multi-acre site, now located within the bounds of the Fingringhoe Wick Nature Discovery Park in Colchester. The site may have been or included a Roman military supply base that was in use until ca. A.D. 120. The site included several structures, a ditched enclosure, and a possible villa.

A series of noncontinuous fortifications are extant on Mount Gildone (elevation 902 meters) that enclose part of an upland plateau. A nucleus of 23 Samnite tombs was also discovered in the vicinity.

Trevinano is a human settlement in Italy, located in the Province of Viterbo of northern Lazio. In antiquity the site was settled by Etruscans. In the eleventh century, the powerful Boncompagni-Ludovisi family built a castle there.

As attested by an inscription found on the site in 1901 and a passage in Ammianus, this fortified country estate was built by one Sammac, son of Nubel, whose brother Firmus assassinated him and raised a revolt against the Romans in the 370s CE. Extensive Roman ruins identified by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas) at a site he called Oum Sekak in the Hassenaoua district of modern Algeria. He estimates the site extent at 13 hectares and reports the remains of a church. An inscription that seems to provide the name of the "genius loci" (Genius Vanisnesi) was found in the vicinity. The site is not clearly visible in twenty-first century aerial/satellite imagery and most of the modern toponymy Gsell provides does not appear in the open-source, digital gazetteers and map tools. The site may now lie under modern development in the area.

Founded by Numidian Berbers, the settlement of Saldae (modern Béjaïa, Algeria) was a minor port during phases of Carthaginian and Roman occupation. The Roman emperor Vespasian established a veteran colony there, at a time when Saldae was part of the province of Mauretania Caesariensis.

As part of the palatial complex of Dūr-Šarrukīn (modern Khorsabad), the eighth-century-BC Assyrian king Sargon II (r. 721–705 BC) constructed six temples, including one to the god Adad.

A town and medieval fortress in northwestern Syria adjacent to the site of ancient Apamea.

An eleventh-century caravanserai along the Silk Road, now located in Uzbekistan. Rabati Malik Caravanserai was built under Karakhanid Shams-al-Mulk Nasr, son of Tamgachkhan Ibragim who ruled in Samarkand from 1068 to 1080. The site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in 2008.
A Roman chamber tomb now located on the grounds of the Policlinico Umberto I hospital in Rome.
Modern day site of a Romano-British settlement in Wiltshire dating from first to fourth centuries A.D.

A modern village in the Refahiye region of Turkey's Erzincan province where remains of ancient roads and routes converge and where a Roman milestone has been found. In Roman times, it was likely a walled town or fort, garrisoned at some point by the cohors I Lepidiana. Scholarly opinions differ as to its possible names in antiquity.
The Temple of Tellus (Thugga) dates to the reign of Gallienus ca. 261 CE.
Another proposed location of ancient Artulu is at or in the vicinity of modern Kayseri.
Find place for cuneiform brick inscription.

An important town of the Middle Elamite period discovered at the archaeological site of Haft Tepe in southwestern Iran. The site was an important center of the Elamite kingdom in the 15th century BCE, and also shows signs of inhabitation from the Parthian to the Early Islamic periods.
Rusahinili (modern Toprakkale) was an ancient fortress of Urartu built by Rusa I.
Castle Dore is a fort located near Fowey in Cornwall that originated in the Iron Age and was re-occupied in the sixth century AD and again during the Middle Ages.
A Middle Helladic to Late Helladic settlement located near Kalloni, Troizenia, Attiki, the Kalloni site was excavated in 2005.

Cissbury Ring is an Iron Age hillfort located north of Worthing in West Sussex, England, and is the second largest hillfort in England. The hillfort, surrounded by earthworks, covers about 24 ha. It was likely abandoned by 50 CE.

While consul in 311 BCE, Caius Iunius Bubulcus Brutus vowed the temple of Salus; he would later dedicate it as dictator in 302 BCE. While no physical remains of the temple are known, textual and epigraphic testimony suggest that it would have been located near the present-day Piazza del Quirinale.

Sepolcro dei Pancrazi is a Roman tomb on the Via Latina dated to the late first or early second century CE. It belonged to a collegium funerarium (funerary college) of the Pancratii, a name attested in two extant inscriptions. Uchi Maius was a township of Africa Proconsularis where Marius settled veterans. It did not achieve the status of colonia until the third century.
Cemetery in modern Turkey's Manisa province with remains from the Early Bronze Age. This is the typesite for the Yortan archaeological culture.
Iron Age fortress in the Northern Negev Desert with a solid wall and ten towers. Inside the fortress are building complexes with streets between them.
A sanctuary with twin temples located at the Etruscan port. The Pyrgi sanctuary was initially excavated by Massimo Pallottino in 1957. The so-called Pyrgi Plaques were discovered here in 1964.
Pyramid and tomb of Pharaoh Amenemhat III of the Twelfth Dynasty.
At Maroni Vournes in southern Cyprus, the remains of a large ashlar building of the thirteenth century BC have been excavated.
Morroni dei Marsi, the remains of two mausolea dating to the Roman period.
Horemheb, final ruler of the 18th dynasty, was buried in KV57.

A settlement mound immediately south of modern Stroviki (municipality of Orchomenos, Thessaly and Central Greece) has yielded archaeological evidence for activity from the Neolithic to the Classical period, with a significant floruit during the Helladic period when the site bordered the northern edge of Lake Copais. Evidence of Mycenean-era hydraulic works involved in the partial draining and control of the lake have been identified in the vicinity.
An elite Gallo-Roman villa with evidence for elaborate gardens dating from the first century CE, now located near the modern French town of Richebourg (Ile-de-France).
Burial site in the modern town of Lapithos in northern Cyprus containing burials dated to the Geometric Period.
The so-called Capitolium temple of the Latin colony of Cosa.
An oppidum of the Statielli/Statellati, where the Romans defeated Ligurian tribes in 173 BC. Its location is not known.
Settlement on the northern shore of Lake Neuchâtel in Switzerland containing the inundated remains of a Bronze Age village, inhabited ca. 1010-955 BC.
Eilean Dòmhnuill is the site of perhaps the earliest crannog settlement in Scotland.

The temple of the god Ninurta, Ehursagtilla (“House Which Exterminates the Mountains”), was located in the Šuanna district (modern Ishin Aswad) of Babylon. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, this was one of two temples in that part of the city, which was located in the southern part of the eastern half of Babylon. The building was rebuilt by the Neo-Babylonian king Nabopolassar (r. 625–605 BC).

The so-called "Kothon" is a large, rectangular, artificial pool dating to the Punic period of Sicily and located on the island of Motya. Originally interpreted as an artificial port basin, recent research reinterpets it as a freshwater basin with functions sacred to the god Ba'al and constituting the central component of a large sanctuary.
A tomb of the Hellenistic period located close to a Graeco-Siceliote center.

Burial ground with 25 graves in 11 mounds located 10km Northeast of Manych, Kalmykia. These graves are largely from the Bronze Age and early Copper Age with some early Iron Age and Medieval graves also present.
Ancient site on the Tigris river in Turkey
Ruins of a Hellenistic courtyard house (possibly connected to the adjacent building, known as Area X) in the archaeological site of Sidi Khiribech in Berenike (modern Benghazi).

A 'Villa rustica' associated with one Caius Olius Ampliatus located in the Ponticelli of Naples, Italy. The site was excavated in 1986-1987, with additional work in 2007. The site covers some 2,000 sq. meters.
La villa rustica di C. Olius Ampliatus

Archaeological site on the banks of the Zerqa River with signs of habitation in the Early Bronze Age I-II and IV. The eastern portion of the larger Tell Um Hammad site is called Um Hammad Sharqiya; the western section is Um Hammad al-Gharbi. The two may have been linked as a single village in the Early Bronze Age IV.
A valley in Egypt where Pharaonic burials took place from the sixteenth to the eleventh centuries B.C. (Eighteenth to the Twentieth Dynasties).
A Medieval tower (12th or 13th century) now located within the grounds of the Caffarella park.
The so-called Columbarium of Constantine is a second century tomb that was later repurposed as a mill.

Ancient Mutina (originally the Etruscan town Mutna), was first inhabited by Villanovans and later by Ligurians and the Gaulish Boii. The Boii sieged the city in 218 BC and later Mutina was re-established as a Roman colony (183 BC). It was an important city and played a role in the civil wars during the last decades of the Roman Republic.

The modern name for a temple built in the south-eastern corner of the Athenian Agora next to the Panathenaic Way in the early second century AD, using material from the Temple of Athena at Sounion. Tell Tweini is an archaeological site located near Jableh, Syria. It was inhabited from the third millennium BC to the Persian period.

The Catacomb of Balbina in the suburbium of Rome lies between the via Appia antica and the via Ardeatina in Rome's Ardeatino district. "I Pini di Sirolo" is the name given to the archaeological site of a Picene necropolis of the first millennium BCE in Italy's Marche region. The necropolis included a large tumulus of the sixth century BCE that included two chariots.
A mosque or madrasa where a stone block with cuneiform inscription was found (and removed) in the 19th Century. The building itself no longer exists.
Sandstone quarries located some 4 km west of Cartagena, in the Diputación de Canteras.
Archaeological site on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea with signs of habitation dated to the Early Bronze Age.
The Casa Herrera Basilica is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida". The paleochristian basilica was built in either the late fifth or early sixth century CE.
Roman Wall and Albarrana Islamic Tower
The Roman Wall and Albarrana Islamic Tower are included in the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida".
Santi Quattro Coronati is an early Christian basilica on Rome's Caelian Hill begun by Pope Miltiades in the fourth century A.D.

The temple of the god Belili, Ekadima (“House Which Creates ...”), was located in the Kumar district of Babylon, in the western half of the inner city. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, it was one of seven temples in that part of Babylon.
A Roman villa dating ca. 50 B.C. located near Monte Gennaro.
A twelfth-century AD Christian church was built atop the remains of the Roman temple of Apollo.
The so-called tomb of Tulliola is a Roman mausoleum located at Formiae. Situated about 100 meters from the so-called tomb of Cicero, this tomb is held to be that of Cicero's father.
Archaeological area of Piano della Comunità

The archaeological area of Piano (or Quarto) di Comunità is an area of Etrusco-Roman Veii where there is evidence for a Republican domus that is modified during the Augustan period. The area is then used as a necropolis in Late Antiquity (fourth and fifth centuries).
A sanctuary complex on the northern margins of ancient Corinth near the theater.
Temple of Asklepios and Lerna Spring
A mound site located approximately 35 km northwest of modern Izmir, Turkey, with signs of habitation from the 3rd millennium BCE through the early Iron Age.
Neolithic burial site located near the eastern bank of the Sarygamysh Lake in modern Turkmenistan, containing remains dated to the 5th-4th millennia BCE.
A Roman fortlet on the Antonine Wall in Scotland.

TT69 is located in the Theban Necropolis on the west bank of the Nile. It served as the tomb of an Egyptian official known as Menna, among whose titles were "Overseer of Fields of Amun", and "Overseer of Fields of the Lord of the Two Lands". The tomb is generally dated to the reign of Thutmosis IV.

A peripteral Doric temple built in the mid-6th c. BCE and destroyed by fire in the 2nd c. BCE. The temple faces east, and was built of mudbrick on foundations of local sandstone, with sandstone column drums and a terracotta roof. A 4th c. BCE dedicatory inscription found in the cella attests the worship of Apollo. The structure was discovered in 1994 following the activity of looters.
The temple of the goddess Gula (as Ninisinna) at Isin. The Sumerian ceremonial name Egalmah means "Exalted Palace."
The second largest of the four islands in Lake Van, in eastern Turkey.
Cathedral of the Holy Cross at Aghtamar
Armenian church built on the island of Aghtamar by King Gagik I Artsruni between 915-921 CE.
A Late Minoan burial site just West of the Knossos Acropolis.
An ancient city of Lower Mesopotamia, Puzriš-Dagan was founded in the twenty-first century B.C. by King Shulgi of Ur.
A fortress in the vicinity of Til-garimmu fortified by the Assyrian king Sargon II (r. 721-705 BC) against Musku (Phrygia).
An early human settlement located in southwestern Turkey. Human occupation began at the site toward the end of the eighth millennium B.C.
Temple of Ba'al (or Bel) in the ancient city of Palmyra.

Main temple in Ahobilam dedicated to the man-lion form of the Hindu god Vishnu built or expanded in the 14th century, sacked by the Mughals in 1578, then restored and expanded at various times up to the present day.
Ptolemaic sanctuary originally situated in Kalabsha, relocated to the southwestern tip of Elephantine Island in 1961.
A hexagonal tomb, perhaps that of a Roman centurion, dating to the late second or early third century AD.
A temple located on the acropolis of Cyrene.
A Neolithic settlement inhabited from ca. 7250 BC to 5000 BC; located in the northwest of Jordan.
The so-called "Terme di Tito" is a terraced Roman villa site located in the modern comune of Castel Sant'Angelo near Lago Paterno.

Nērebtum is a medium-sized Bronze Age settlement located east of Baghdad on the left bank of the Diyala river. Nērebtum was inhabited from the third to the early second millennium BCE. Excavations at the site by the University of Chicago from 1934 to 1936 exposed two extensive temple structures, one dedicated to the moon god Sîn, another to the goddess Ištar-Kititum, along with extensive fortification walls and private houses.
Erek Dağ is a mountain in the Van Province in eastern Anatolia. It is the second-highest peak of the province of Van, rising to 3200 meters above sea level.
Tell al-Rimah, is the site of a settlement inhabited from the third to first millennium BCE that has been identified as the site of either Qattara or Karana.
A communal tomb dated to 424 BCE that was once crowned by a lion.
The basilica of Santa Balbina is a paleo-Christian basilica in Rome, located on the "little Aventine".

The house of Lucius Fabius Cilo, praefectus urbi in 203, consul in 193 and 204, and a close friend of the emperor Septimius Severus. The house was a gift of the Severans and appears on the Severan marble plan. Its site is now occupied by the basilica of Santa Balbina on the "little Aventine".
The Eaton House Roman Fort was a Roman auxiliary fort located just outside Pennocrucium.
Remains of a Roman fort have been identified at Blennerhasset on the River Ellen.
The tomb of the boy poet Quintus Sulpicius Maximus on the Via Salaria in Rome. He died in 94 CE, aged just 11 years.

The temple of the god Išhara, Ešasurra (“House of the Womb”), was located in the Šuanna district (modern Ishin Aswad) of Babylon. According to the Babylonian topographical text Tintir = Babylon Tablet IV, this was one of two temples in that part of the city, which was located in the southern part of the eastern half of Babylon.
An archaeological site in the Central Taurus Mountains dated to the early Bronze Age. The Göltepe hill contains traces of a village associated with the nearby mine site of Kestel.

Flower's Barrow hill fort overlooks Worbarrow Bay in Dorset on England's south coast.
Kayalıdere Castle is a fortified Urartian site dating to the eighth century BCE. It is located in the Varto district of Muş.
An ancient settlement mound located within the boundaries of modern Yiğittaşı, Turkey, in eastern Anatolia.
A temple of Hercules located near the Circus Maximus.
Cadbury Castle, Devon an Iron Age Hillfort located near Bickleigh, Devon, England. The site was reused during the English Civil War.
A small Gallo-Roman settlement south of Béziers, located on the coast at La Fount de Rome.
